terms.definition: The process of making illegally-obtained proceeds appear legal by disguising the true nature, source, location, ownership, or control of the funds.
The underlying criminal activity that generates proceeds which are then laundered. Examples: drug trafficking, fraud, corruption, tax evasion.
First stage of ML: Introducing illicit cash into the financial system through deposits, purchases, or other means.
Second stage of ML: Creating complex layers of financial transactions to separate illicit proceeds from their source and obscure the audit trail.
Third stage of ML: Reintroducing laundered funds into the legitimate economy through seemingly normal business or personal transactions.
Providing or collecting funds to be used for terrorist acts. Unlike ML, funds may come from legitimate sources. The goal is to hide the PURPOSE of funds, not their SOURCE.
Breaking up large cash transactions into smaller amounts to avoid reporting thresholds (e.g., $10,000 in the US). Itself a federal crime.
A form of structuring using very small amounts, often below $3,000, to avoid even the CTR and recordkeeping thresholds.
An arrangement where one bank (correspondent) provides services on behalf of another bank (respondent), often to access the financial system of a foreign country.
The bank that uses the correspondent bank's services to access foreign financial systems. The correspondent bank must perform due diligence on the respondent.
An account at a correspondent bank that allows the respondent bank's customers to directly conduct transactions, creating higher ML risk than standard correspondent arrangements.
When a respondent bank allows other banks to use its correspondent banking relationship without the correspondent bank's knowledge, creating hidden sub-relationships.
Internal bank accounts used to facilitate processing and settlement of multiple customer transactions, often on the same day. Can obscure customer identity if not properly managed.
Personalized financial services for high-net-worth individuals. Higher ML risk due to personal relationships, complex structures, and confidentiality expectations.
An individual entrusted with a prominent public function (e.g., head of state, senior politician, military leader). Includes family members and close associates. Requires Enhanced Due Diligence.
A company that has no active business operations, significant assets, or employees. Often used to obscure beneficial ownership and move illicit funds.
A company that was legally formed but has remained inactive ('on the shelf'). Purchased to provide an appearance of longevity and legitimacy.
The natural person(s) who ultimately owns or controls a legal entity or arrangement, or on whose behalf a transaction is conducted. Key concept in transparency.
Non-bank financial institution providing services like money transmission, check cashing, currency exchange, or selling money orders/travelers checks.
An informal value transfer system based on trust and personal networks. Transfers value without physically moving money. Common in South Asia and Middle East.
Systems for transferring money/value outside the conventional banking system. Includes hawala, hundi, fei ch'ien. Often unregulated or under-regulated.
Using international trade transactions to disguise and move value. Techniques include over/under-invoicing, multiple invoicing, and misrepresentation of goods/services.
A trade-based ML method originally from Colombian drug trade. Converts drug dollars in the US into pesos in Colombia through trade transactions.
Designated areas within a country where goods may be imported, stored, handled, and re-exported without customs duties. Reduced oversight creates ML vulnerabilities.
Professionals who control access to the financial system: lawyers, notaries, accountants, auditors. Can facilitate or prevent ML through their professional services.
Professionals who create and manage legal entities and arrangements (companies, trusts). Can be exploited to create complex structures hiding beneficial ownership.
A digital representation of value that can be digitally traded and functions as a medium of exchange, unit of account, or store of value. Includes cryptocurrency.
Any person/entity that conducts exchange, transfer, safekeeping, or administration of virtual assets. Subject to FATF standards since 2019.
A stored value card loaded with funds in advance. ML risk due to anonymity, ease of cross-border transport, and difficulty tracing transactions.
Organizations that raise/disburse funds for charitable, religious, or social purposes. Vulnerable to TF abuse through diversion of funds or sham entities.
Deliberate avoidance of knowledge of the facts; courts treat it as the equivalent of actual knowledge for ML offenses. Also called 'purposeful indifference'.
Illegal trade in protected animal and plant species. Increasingly recognized as a significant predicate offense for money laundering.
Intergovernmental body established in 1989 by G7 to set international AML/CFT standards. Issues the 40 Recommendations and conducts mutual evaluations.
The international standards for combating ML, TF, and proliferation financing. Cover legal systems, law enforcement, financial system, transparency, and international cooperation.
Detailed implementation guidance published alongside each FATF Recommendation. Provide specifics on how to implement the standards.
The foundational principle that countries and institutions should identify, assess, and understand their ML/TF risks and apply commensurate measures. FATF R.1.
A peer review process where FATF or FSRB members assess a country's compliance with the 40 Recommendations and the effectiveness of its AML/CFT system.
Countries identified as having strategic deficiencies in their AML/CFT regimes but have committed to action plans. Formally: 'Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring'.
Countries with significant strategic deficiencies that have not committed to action plans. Formally: 'High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action'. Triggers countermeasures.
Regional organizations that promote FATF standards in their regions and conduct mutual evaluations. Examples: APG, CFATF, MONEYVAL, GAFILAT.
Global standard-setter for bank regulation. Issued key AML guidance including KYC paper (2001), Sound Management of ML/TF Risks, and Correspondent Banking annex.
Series of directives (1st through 6th) establishing EU-wide AML/CFT requirements. Each expanded scope, covered entities, and requirements.
International network of Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs). Facilitates cooperation and information exchange among FIUs worldwide through the Egmont Secure Web.
Association of 13 global banks that develop frameworks and guidance for managing financial crime risks. Published Wolfsberg Principles on AML, KYC, and correspondent banking.
Uniting and Strengthening America by Providing Appropriate Tools Required to Intercept and Obstruct Terrorism Act of 2001. Key US AML legislation post-9/11.
Authorizes Treasury to designate foreign jurisdictions, institutions, or transactions as 'primary money laundering concerns' and impose special measures.
Requires enhanced due diligence for correspondent accounts and private banking accounts held by non-US persons.
Allows law enforcement to request financial institutions to search their records for accounts of persons suspected of terrorism or ML.
Provides safe harbor for financial institutions to share information with each other to identify and report ML or TF, under specific conditions.
Requires financial institutions to establish Customer Identification Programs (CIP) to verify identity of persons opening accounts.
Major update to US AML framework. Established beneficial ownership reporting, enhanced whistleblower protections, and expanded BSA coverage to virtual currency.
US federal law (1970) requiring financial institutions to maintain records and file reports to assist government agencies in detecting and preventing ML.
US Treasury bureau administering economic/trade sanctions. Maintains the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. Violations carry strict liability.
Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List maintained by OFAC. Individuals and entities whose assets must be blocked; transactions with them are prohibited.
Entities owned 50% or more, directly or indirectly, by one or more blocked persons are themselves considered blocked, even if not listed on the SDN List.
UN Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs. First international treaty to define money laundering as a criminal offense.
UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime. Broadened the definition of money laundering beyond drug trafficking to all serious crimes.
Non-financial entities subject to AML/CFT obligations: casinos, real estate agents, dealers in precious metals/stones, lawyers, notaries, accountants, TCSPs.
FSRB for the Asia-Pacific region. 41 member jurisdictions. Conducts mutual evaluations and typologies research.
FSRB for the Caribbean basin region. 25+ member states.
Committee of Experts on the Evaluation of Anti-Money Laundering Measures and the Financing of Terrorism. FSRB for Council of Europe member states not in FATF.
Financial Action Task Force of Latin America. FSRB for Latin American countries. Formerly GAFISUD.
Financial Crimes Enforcement Network. US FIU within the Treasury Department. Collects and analyzes financial transaction data to combat ML, TF, and other financial crimes.
The process of identifying and verifying customer identity, understanding the nature of customer activities, and assessing ML/TF risks. Foundation of KYC.
Additional measures applied to higher-risk customers, products, or geographies. Required for PEPs, correspondent banking, and complex/unusual transactions.
Reduced CDD measures permitted for lower-risk situations where ML/TF risk is assessed as low. Not allowed when there is suspicion of ML/TF.
Comprehensive framework for understanding who customers are, what they do, and what is normal for them. Includes CDD, ongoing monitoring, and risk assessment.
Program to screen employees for ML/TF risk, including background checks, monitoring for unusual behavior, and creating a culture of compliance.
US requirement (Section 326) for financial institutions to verify the identity of persons opening accounts using documentary or non-documentary methods.
Mandatory filing with FIU when a financial institution knows, suspects, or has reason to suspect ML, TF, or other suspicious activity. Confidential -- no tipping off.
US report filed for cash transactions exceeding $10,000 in a single business day. Filed with FinCEN.
Illegally disclosing to a customer or others that a SAR has been or will be filed, or that an investigation is underway. Criminal offense in most jurisdictions.
Legal protection for financial institutions and employees who file SARs in good faith, shielding them from liability even if the reported activity turns out to be legitimate.
Senior employee designated with responsibility for the institution's AML/CFT compliance program. Must have sufficient authority, independence, and access to resources.
Regular review of the AML/CFT program by qualified persons independent of the compliance function. Tests adequacy and effectiveness of the program.
Required education for all relevant employees on ML/TF risks, regulations, institution policies, and their obligations. Must be ongoing and role-appropriate.
An organizational environment where compliance is valued, supported by senior management ('tone from the top'), and embedded in daily operations.
Ongoing surveillance of customer transactions to detect patterns or activities that may indicate ML, TF, or other suspicious activity. Can be manual or automated.
Process of checking customers, transactions, and counterparties against sanctions lists (OFAC SDN, UN, EU, etc.) to ensure compliance with sanctions programs.
Process of identifying whether customers or their associates are Politically Exposed Persons, triggering EDD requirements.
Methodology for assigning risk ratings to customers based on factors like geography, product type, transaction patterns, and customer type. Drives the level of due diligence.
Core elements: (1) Internal policies/procedures/controls, (2) Compliance officer, (3) Training, (4) Independent testing. US adds (5) Risk-based CDD including beneficial ownership.
Continuous review of customer activity to ensure transactions are consistent with the institution's knowledge of the customer, their business, and risk profile.
Indicators of potentially suspicious activity that may warrant further investigation. Categories include unusual behavior, transactions, identification, and employee activity.
Practice of financial institutions terminating or restricting business relationships with entire categories of customers perceived as high-risk, rather than managing the risk.
Requirement that originator and beneficiary information accompany wire transfers throughout the payment chain. Based on FATF R.16.
Technology systems for transaction monitoring, sanctions screening, and risk scoring. Require proper calibration to balance detection with false positive management.
Term used in many jurisdictions outside the US for reports of suspicious activity (equivalent to SAR). Filed with the national FIU.
National agency responsible for receiving, analyzing, and disseminating suspicious transaction reports. Three core functions: Receive, Analyze, Disseminate.
Bilateral agreement between countries for exchanging evidence and legal assistance in criminal investigations. Formal mechanism for international cooperation.
Sharing Electronic Resources and Laws on Crime. UN knowledge management portal for ML information maintained by UNODC.
Legal order requiring production of documents or testimony. Financial institutions must have systems to respond while protecting privileged information.
FinCEN request to financial institutions to search records for accounts of specific persons suspected of terrorism or ML. Must be searched within 14 days.
Conducting an internal investigation simultaneously with a government/law enforcement investigation. Requires careful coordination and legal guidance.
Decision to close a customer's account due to suspicious activity or inability to manage ML/TF risk. Must be documented and may trigger SAR filing.
Letters rogatory or formal request from one country's court to another country's court for judicial assistance in obtaining evidence.
Agreement between FIUs or regulators to cooperate and share information. Less formal than MLATs. Used for intelligence (not evidence) sharing.
Decentralized EU network for FIUs to exchange information, using features like Ma3tch for matching common subjects without exposing irrelevant data.
Secure communication channel used by Egmont Group member FIUs to exchange information about suspicious transactions.
Legal protection of communications between client and attorney. In internal investigations, applies to the entity, not individual employees. Can be waived.
Detailed record of documents withheld from production due to attorney-client privilege or work product doctrine during an investigation.
Providing funds or financial services for the manufacture, acquisition, or development of weapons of mass destruction (WMD). Covered by FATF R.7.
Freezing assets and prohibiting financial transactions with designated persons/entities related to terrorism (R.6) or WMD proliferation (R.7).
FATF R.13 requires institutions to understand the respondent's business, assess its AML/CFT controls, obtain senior management approval, and prohibit relationships with shell banks.
FATF R.16 requirement that originator and beneficiary information travel with wire transfers. Extended to virtual asset transfers in 2019.
FATF R.11 requires maintaining transaction records and CDD information for at least 5 years after the relationship ends or transaction date.
FATF R.20 requires reporting suspicious transactions to FIU regardless of amount, including attempted transactions. No threshold applies.
The ability of a country (notably the US) to prosecute ML offenses that have a connection to that country, even if the primary conduct occurred elsewhere.

fatf_recs.title: Risk-Based Approach
fatf_recs.key_points: Countries must assess risks and apply commensurate measures. Foundation for all other recommendations.

fatf_recs.title: National Cooperation and Coordination
fatf_recs.key_points: Countries should have national AML/CFT policies and designate authority for coordination.

fatf_recs.title: Money Laundering Offense
fatf_recs.key_points: Criminalize ML based on Vienna and Palermo Conventions. Broad interpretation of 'knowing'.

fatf_recs.title: Confiscation and Provisional Measures
fatf_recs.key_points: Enable confiscation of laundered property, proceeds, and instrumentalities.

fatf_recs.title: Terrorist Financing Offense
fatf_recs.key_points: Criminalize TF on basis of TF Convention. Applies regardless of whether funds were actually used.

fatf_recs.title: Targeted Financial Sanctions - Terrorism
fatf_recs.key_points: Implement UN Security Council Resolutions on terrorism. Freeze assets without delay.

fatf_recs.title: Targeted Financial Sanctions - Proliferation
fatf_recs.key_points: Implement UNSC resolutions on WMD proliferation financing (North Korea, Iran).

fatf_recs.title: Non-Profit Organizations
fatf_recs.key_points: Protect NPOs from TF abuse using risk-based approach. Revised 2023 to prevent disproportionate measures.

fatf_recs.title: Financial Institution Secrecy Laws
fatf_recs.key_points: Bank secrecy must not inhibit implementation of FATF Recommendations.

fatf_recs.title: Customer Due Diligence
fatf_recs.key_points: THE most important rec. Identify/verify customers, beneficial owners. Understand purpose of relationship. Ongoing monitoring.

fatf_recs.title: Record-keeping
fatf_recs.key_points: Maintain transaction records and CDD info for at least 5 years.

fatf_recs.title: Politically Exposed Persons
fatf_recs.key_points: Require EDD for PEPs (foreign, domestic, international org). Includes family and close associates.

fatf_recs.title: Correspondent Banking
fatf_recs.key_points: Assess respondent's AML/CFT controls. Senior management approval. Prohibit shell bank relationships.

fatf_recs.title: Money/Value Transfer Services
fatf_recs.key_points: MVT providers must be licensed/registered and comply with AML/CFT measures.

fatf_recs.title: New Technologies (Virtual Assets)
fatf_recs.key_points: Apply RBA to virtual assets and VASPs. VASPs must be licensed/registered. Crypto travel rule.

fatf_recs.title: Wire Transfers (Travel Rule)
fatf_recs.key_points: Originator and beneficiary info must accompany wire transfers. Ordering, intermediary, and beneficiary institution obligations.

fatf_recs.title: Reliance on Third Parties
fatf_recs.key_points: FIs may rely on third parties for CDD but remain ultimately responsible.

fatf_recs.title: Internal Controls
fatf_recs.key_points: FIs must implement AML/CFT programs: compliance officer, training, independent audit, screening procedures. Group-wide programs.

fatf_recs.title: Higher-Risk Countries
fatf_recs.key_points: Apply enhanced measures proportionate to risks for countries on FATF grey/black lists.

fatf_recs.title: Suspicious Transaction Reporting
fatf_recs.key_points: File STRs/SARs with FIU for suspected ML/TF. No monetary threshold. Includes attempted transactions.

fatf_recs.title: Tipping-Off and Confidentiality
fatf_recs.key_points: FIs and their employees protected from liability for good-faith reporting. Prohibited from disclosing ('tipping off').

fatf_recs.title: DNFBPs: CDD
fatf_recs.key_points: Apply CDD requirements to designated non-financial businesses and professions.

fatf_recs.title: DNFBPs: Other Measures
fatf_recs.key_points: Apply reporting, internal controls, and other preventive measures to DNFBPs.

fatf_recs.title: Transparency of Legal Persons
fatf_recs.key_points: Countries must ensure adequate transparency of beneficial ownership of legal persons. 2022 revision strengthened requirements.

fatf_recs.title: Transparency of Legal Arrangements
fatf_recs.key_points: Ensure adequate transparency of beneficial ownership of trusts and similar arrangements.

fatf_recs.title: Regulation and Supervision of FIs
fatf_recs.key_points: FIs must be subject to adequate AML/CFT regulation and supervision. Risk-based supervisory approach.

fatf_recs.title: Powers of Supervisors
fatf_recs.key_points: Supervisors must have adequate powers to supervise, inspect, compel production, and impose sanctions.

fatf_recs.title: Regulation of DNFBPs
fatf_recs.key_points: DNFBPs subject to regulation and supervision for AML/CFT compliance.

fatf_recs.title: Financial Intelligence Units
fatf_recs.key_points: Countries should establish FIUs to receive, analyze, and disseminate STRs and other relevant information.

fatf_recs.title: Law Enforcement Responsibilities
fatf_recs.key_points: Designated law enforcement authorities must investigate ML, TF, and predicate offenses.

fatf_recs.title: Powers of Law Enforcement
fatf_recs.key_points: Powers to compel production, search, seize, take witness statements, use investigative techniques.

fatf_recs.title: Cash Couriers
fatf_recs.key_points: Detect physical cross-border transportation of currency and bearer negotiable instruments.

fatf_recs.title: Statistics
fatf_recs.key_points: Maintain comprehensive statistics on AML/CFT effectiveness.

fatf_recs.title: Guidance and Feedback
fatf_recs.key_points: Competent authorities should provide guidance and feedback to FIs and DNFBPs.

fatf_recs.title: Sanctions
fatf_recs.key_points: Effective proportionate and dissuasive sanctions for non-compliance with AML/CFT requirements.

fatf_recs.title: International Instruments
fatf_recs.key_points: Become party to and implement relevant international conventions (Vienna, Palermo, TF Convention).

fatf_recs.title: Mutual Legal Assistance
fatf_recs.key_points: Provide widest range of mutual legal assistance in ML/TF investigations and prosecutions.

fatf_recs.title: MLA: Freezing and Confiscation
fatf_recs.key_points: Enable freezing and confiscation of assets at foreign request.

fatf_recs.title: Extradition
fatf_recs.key_points: Cooperate on extradition for ML and TF offenses.

fatf_recs.title: Other Forms of International Cooperation
fatf_recs.key_points: Exchange information spontaneously and upon request with foreign counterparts.
